title: When Bigger Becomes Brittle: Why Compression Hurts More as Language Models Scale
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 5 Nov 2026]
Title:When Bigger Becomes Brittle: Why Compression Hurts More as Language Models Scale
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Quantization and pruning reduce the cost of deploying language models, but their effects are usually reported as benchmark scores. Such scores record only the loss that remains at the output. Inside the model, compression damages some components more than others, and the rest of the network can partly compensate. The observed loss therefore reflects both the damage and this compensation, which benchmark scores cannot separate. How the two combine, and whether their balance changes with model size, remains unclear. We study this compensation for in-context retrieval, a capability carried by a small, identifiable set of attention heads. To separate the two, the expected loss from ablating these heads is decomposed exactly into the part restored by the rest of the network, attributed to the components responsible, and the part that reaches the output. This decomposition is then compared across model sizes. For damage of comparable size, smaller models restore most of the loss, whereas larger models retain most of it, because the compensating responses offset less of it as models grow. Compressing the heads produces the same pattern. Compression that is nearly harmless in small models can therefore be costly in large ones.

report.summary: A new study finds quantization and pruning can be nearly harmless in small language models but disproportionately costly in larger ones, because larger models compensate less for internal damage.
report.background: Quantization and pruning are widely used to cut the memory, latency, and serving cost of large language models. Their effects are usually judged by benchmark scores, which capture only the final output loss after the rest of the network has partially compensated for damaged components. That makes compression look safer than it may be internally. The paper studies in-context retrieval, a capability linked to a small, identifiable set of attention heads, and asks whether the balance between local damage and network-wide compensation changes as models scale. The finding matters because deployment teams often assume compression behaves similarly across model sizes, while vendors and users rely on aggregate scores to decide whether a compressed model is safe to ship.
key_points: Benchmark scores obscure what happens inside a compressed model. They show only the loss that survives after undamaged components partially compensate for damaged ones, so two models with similar scores may have very different internal fragility. The paper argues that damage and compensation must be separated to understand compression risk.

The authors isolate in-context retrieval by studying a small set of attention heads. They exactly decompose the expected loss from ablating or compressing those heads into the portion restored by the rest of the network and the portion that reaches the output, then compare this decomposition across model sizes.

The scaling pattern is the central result: for comparable damage, smaller models restore most of the lost capability, while larger models retain most of the loss. As models grow, compensating responses offset less of the damage, so the same intervention becomes more harmful.

Compressing the retrieval heads produces the same pattern as ablation. This means compression that appears nearly harmless in a small model can be costly in a large one, challenging the assumption that quantization and pruning scale safely by default.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the result challenges a common deployment shortcut: assuming a compression recipe validated on smaller models will transfer safely to larger ones. Model providers may need size-aware compression evaluations and internal diagnostics, not just aggregate benchmark scores. Developers should test task-specific capabilities such as in-context retrieval and long-context use after quantization or pruning, especially on larger models. For regular users, the practical risk is subtler degradation in retrieval-heavy or context-dependent tasks even when headline scores look acceptable. The paper does not reject compression, but it shows that larger models can be more brittle under comparable damage, so compression budgets and evaluation suites should be recalibrated as models scale.
report.tools: No paper-specific code is listed, but readers can follow up with open-source compression stacks such as GPTQ, AWQ, bitsandbytes, SparseGPT, and LLM-Pruner, plus Hugging Face Transformers and Optimum for evaluation. These tools support post-training quantization and pruning; compare damage and compensation across model sizes and test in-context retrieval rather than relying only on aggregate benchmarks.
